extracted.intended_audience: Department of Defense productivity analysts, military medical managers, DPPO/BLS staff, and defense policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and measurement standards for computing and using the Composite Work Unit / Adjusted Admission Equivalents and related productivity indices for U.S. military medical services. Covers metric definitions, formulas, weighting/base-year computation, data submissions, uses, and criticisms/limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBD (Occupied Bed Days) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: OBD is computed as the total occupied bed days per fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used historically as a workload indicator (total inpatient days). Reference: Ref. 16: p. XV-1-3.

rubrics_metrics.name: AD (Admissions) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An admission is the state of one patient becoming an inpatient at a facility which provides inpatient medical care. AD is computed by total admissions for a fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions count each new inpatient admission; used as an input element in product measures. Reference: Ref. 16: p. IV-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: LB (Live Births) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Live Births: an admission of a newborn with mother when the birth occurred at the mother's admitting facility. LB is computed by total births in a fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts births occurring at the admitting facility; included as a distinct output element. Reference: Ref. 16: p. IV-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPV (Outpatient Visits) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Outpatient visit: the act of a patient going to an organized or specialty clinic in an outpatient status for examination, diagnosis, or medical advice. OPV is the total number of outpatient visits in a fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes inpatient clinical visits for non-related admission problems and telephone consultations if an entry is made in the patient's chart; classification depends on medical care provided rather than professional level. Reference: Ref. 17: p. 4-8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence adjustments in Composite Work Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalences used to convert heterogeneous workload elements into a common unit: one admission was determined equal to the same staffing requirements as 10 occupied bed days; one live birth equal to 10 patient days; three outpatient visits equal approximately one occupied bed day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences were introduced to account for varying length-of-stay, newborn care requirements, and to better quantify outpatient resource use (Ref. 18: p. 2-4). They underpin the Composite Work Unit concept as an improvement over raw OBD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outpatient weight adjustment (.30 to .25) (tri-service variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1967 the Air Force changed the outpatient workload weight from 0.30 to 0.25 because the higher weight was believed to over-evaluate outpatient visits relative to inpatient care and resource requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modification affected only how the Air Force computed the Composite Work Unit; the Army and Navy continued using the 0.30 weight factor (Ref. 19). Highlights that service-specific weighting choices alter comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusted Admission Equivalent (AAE) formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of AAEs = ADM + .0150 PV + .016 DP + .003 LP + .002 PR + .004 XR
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where ADM = total admissions; PV (presumably outpatient visits); DP = total dental visits; LP = total laboratory procedures; PR = total pharmaceutical prescriptions; XR = total x-rays processed. Hospitals without dental services exclude the dental portion. Clinic AAEs computed similarly for clinics with/without dental services. AAE relies solely on number of admissions for inpatient workload rather than occupied bed days (Ref. 15: p. 4-5).

rubrics_metrics.name: AAE use / reporting distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Air Force uses the AAE for internal purposes and reports Composite Work Units for external purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite literature claims, indices reported by DPPO and BLS for Air Force medical services actually consist of indices established with AAEs. Exhibits show productivity indices computed with AAE-based outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to weighted output using base-year weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured output is converted into a weighted output using base year weights and reported by facility type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base year (1977 in exhibits) weights are established by equalizing the output to the employee-years element so that weighted output and employee-years in the base year are numerically equal. For trend analysis, outputs are multiplied by base weights to create weighted outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-year normalization / percentage presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a base year (1977) was established, all input elements are set at 100.000 (100 percent); each succeeding year's input element is converted to a percentage based on the base year's gross numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On exhibits, items are presented as percentages relative to the base year rather than gross numbers. This standardizes inputs for trend computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity index computation (per employee-year)
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity per employee-year is computed by dividing the weighted output (A) by the employee-years (B), both based on their respective percentages relative to base year values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other indices (e.g., compensation/employee-years, unit labor cost) are computed similarly. This is the standard arithmetic for deriving productivity indices from weighted outputs and inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured activities vs total activities distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits are divided into two sections: measured activities and total activities (which contains measured, non-measured, and support activities required to produce the indicated output quantity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total activities include additional input components beyond directly measured activities; analysts should be aware which set is used for a given productivity computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: DPPO dual data set practice
rubrics_metrics.description: DPPO maintains a dual database: one set of data is considered 'acceptable' and submitted to the Bureau of Labor Statistics for productivity computations; another set is maintained by DPPO for internal management visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two data sets serve different audiences/purposes; indices returned by BLS are used by submitting agencies whereas DPPO uses its internal set for trend visualization across ~40 functions (Ref. 11: p. 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation into Federal Composite Work Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite Work Unit data from all federal agencies providing medical services are aggregated into a Federal Composite Work Unit, allowing federal medical productivity indices to be computed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further aggregation of product measurement units across non-medical functions (28 groups) produces an overall federal government productivity index, normally published (e.g., Handbook for Labor Statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of the Composite Work Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally used to replace occupied bed days for manpower allocation; also used for internal management, staffing, developing medical programs, supply and overhead cost in budgeting, and cross-hospital cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CWU provides a single unit measure intended to capture fluctuating workload for many managerial purposes (Ref. 15: p. 3-4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of statistical data to DPPO
rubrics_metrics.description: Military services submit statistical data for workload measurement to DPPO, including Composite Work Unit calculations, total manhours, and employee compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DPPO computes productivity indices for medical services using submitted data and returns computations to the submitting agencies for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: CWU does not distinguish necessary vs unnecessary occupied bed days
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit 'makes no distinction between a 'necessary' occupied bed day and an 'unnecessary' occupied bed day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary occupied bed days increase average daily occupied bed day input and inflate the total CWU and measured productivity; this is a key limitation noted by Naval Medical Data Services Center (Ref. 22: pp. 5-6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: CWU insensitive to changing length of stay
rubrics_metrics.description: CWU method lacks a built-in factor to account for changes in average length of stay; decreases in length of stay can reduce occupied bed days and thus appear to lower productivity even if effort per patient rose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: average inpatient length of stay declined from 12.68 days (1973) to 5.92 days (1979), reducing occupied bed days by 57.3% and affecting CWU computations and perceived productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: CWU assumes equivalence of occupied bed days across patients
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit assumes all occupied bed days are equivalent, though patients require differing amounts of care based on illness severity, age, sex, and complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption can mask increases in effort per patient (e.g., more intensive care but shorter stays) and thus suggest a decrease in productivity despite higher per-patient work (Ref. 15: p. 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tri-service finding on staff utilization over hospital stay
rubrics_metrics.description: A tri-service study concluded that the initial 3 to 5 days of an inpatient stay required approximately 10 times the staff utilization for later periods of hospitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: CWU and similar measures that treat bed-days equally fail to account for front-loaded staffing needs and patient turnover; staffing needs for short-stay hospitals should be viewed from turnover perspective, not simply CWU (Ref. 19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval study adjustment method (example procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study computed adjusted results by: (1) taking two years for comparison (1973 and 1979); (2) adjusting occupied bed days to correspond with 1979 length of stay; (3) computing CWUs for both years; and (4) adjusting both years by the American Hospital Association's 'Hospital Intensity Index.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure produced adjusted CWUs and demonstrated an actual increase in productivity when accounting for length-of-stay changes and service intensity (Ref. 22: pp. 9, 14). Exhibit V demonstrates differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospital Intensity Index (HII) use and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hospital Intensity Index is a weighted average of hospital input components based on period input prices so that changes in the index are proportional to their importance in overall input cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though HII has drawbacks as a conversion factor for CWU, the study noted it 'may be useful in adjusting more traditional workload indicators for service intensity' (Ref. 22: p. 14). Analysts may apply HII to adjust workload indicators for intensity differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service-specific computation notes (dental omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hospitals without dental services exclude the dental portion (DP) of the AAE computation; clinics compute AAE similarly with or without dental services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure facility-type-specific components are included/excluded consistently when computing AAEs and aggregating outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caution when comparing military and private-sector indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing DoD productivity indices with private sector indices has inherent problems due to differences in covered activities, measurement methodologies, and measurement concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should be cautious about cross-sector comparisons; BLS produces civilian-sector indices (e.g., Monthly Labor Review) which do not include federal government data (Ref. 11: pp. 13-15).
